messages.subject: more than 5 correlated random effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

as far as I understand, this is the inla formula for a model with 5 correlated random effects:

inla_5_correlated_re = y ~ A + B + C + C +
                                           f(group1, model = "idd5d", n = 5*length(unique(my_data$group1))  +
                                           f(group2, A, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group3, B, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group4, C, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group5, D, copy = "group1")

Is this correct?

If yes, does this mean that one cannot estimate more than 5 correlated random effects in INLA, because inla knows up to 5 dimensional iids?

Given the documentation here https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/latent/iid.pdf,  I assume that this model estimates the covariance between all random effects.

If it is not possible to estimate the full covariance of all random effects in inla, would it be possible to specify a model that estimates the covariance between the intercept and the other random effects, e.g. like this:

inla_5_partially_correlated_re = y ~ A + B + C + C + D + E
                                           f(group1, model = "idd2d", n = 5*length(unique(my_data$group1))  +
                                           f(group2, A, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group3, B, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group4, C, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group5, D, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group6, C, copy = "group1")  +
                                           f(group7, C, copy = "group1")

(inla accepts and fits such a model, but I am not sure which covariance is estimates here.)

Thanks in advance!
Guido

Hello,

as far as I understand, this is the inla formula for a model with 5 correlated random effects:

inla_5_correlated_re = y ~ A + B + C + C +

                                           f(group1, model = "idd5d", n = 5*length(unique(my_data$group1))  +

                                           f(group2, A, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group3, B, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group4, C, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group5, D, copy = "group1")

Is this correct?

If yes, does this mean that one cannot estimate more than 5 correlated random effects in INLA, because inla knows up to 5 dimensional iids?

Given the documentation here https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/latent/iid.pdf,  I assume that this model estimates the covariance between all random effects.

If it is not possible to estimate the full covariance of all random effects in inla, would it be possible to specify a model that estimates the covariance between the intercept and the other random effects, e.g. like this:

inla_5_partially_correlated_re = y ~ A + B + C + C + D + E

                                           f(group1, model = "idd2d", n = 5*length(unique(my_data$group1))  +

                                           f(group2, A, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group3, B, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group4, C, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group5, D, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group6, C, copy = "group1")  +

                                           f(group7, C, copy = "group1")

(inla accepts and fits such a model, but I am not sure which covariance is estimates here.)

Thanks in advance!

Guido

in this case that takes the left endpoint above 0. The extra
probability from 0.95 to 0.96985 is the probability mass between 0 and
the left endpoint of the one-sided interval.
So yes, 1-pmarginal is the probability of exceeding 0.

Finn

Hello group list,

Thanks for providing this space to seek advice.

I am new to INLA and have a few questions mostly trying to figure out why adding an AR1 component to a spatial spde Poisson model causes many CPO failures.
While only including the spde spatial term results in almost no failures.
I also have a couple of questions about specifying priors that I will intersperse in the code below.

Project:
I am modelling the population recovery of a dove species following a hurricane on an island. I have counts of birds at points across the island with unequal sampling effort across the years.
Most points are repeated, however, the actual coordinates of repeated points change slightly each year due to accessibility and GPS error.

Data:
> head(wwd.dat[,c(3:11,18:19)])
   Sample_Lab.x      lat       lon    month year size     urban   veg_height   moisture        x                 y
1        GC29  19.35600 -81.27587     9         1    1    2.713082 -0.5742221 -0.4829225 471.0126 2140.034
2        GC69  19.28085 -81.25305     9         1    3    1.713082  2.4257779 -0.4829225 472.7939 2140.743
3        GC113 19.34227 -81.37787     9        1    0    2.713082 -0.5742221 -0.4829225 478.6616 2138.319
4        GC114 19.33763 -81.37310     9        1    0    2.713082 -0.5742221 -0.4829225 483.1879 2139.441
5        GC115 19.32815 -81.37247     9        1    0    2.713082 -0.5742221 -0.4829225 489.6800 2138.996
6        GC117 19.31733 -81.36918     9        1    0   -1.286918  2.4257779  3.5170775 481.2433 2134.562

Here is a subset of the data - the counts are birds are in the size column, the covariates urban, veg_height, and moisture are centred, and x and y are UTM coordinates in Km.

The count data is mostly 0's and 1's with a few counts up to 10 and then two large outliers of 30 and 42.
> summary(wwd.dat$size)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  0.000   0.000   0.000   1.414   2.000  42.000

The distribution of sampled points across years is:
> table(wwd.dat$year)

  1     2   3     7
111 126  95 132

Index of year group to be used later
n_year <- max(wwd.dat$year)

The surveys were done regularly at the start but then there is a 4 year gap between the last year and the previous survey (I am using a subset of the data for now - I do have data for years 9, 11, 14).

Spatiotemporal model set up:

#creating mesh
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc=as.matrix(wwd.dat[,18:19]), boundary=domainGC, cutoff=0.5,max.edge = c(1,50)*0.5)

# matern covariance
spde  <-  inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh=mesh, alpha=2,
  prior.range = c(15, 0.0001), #range of the spatial effect
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.0001))  # variance of the spatial effect

The island I am working on has a length of 35 km so my intention with these priors is to be vague. I've noticed that the help page for this function does not include prior.range or prior.sigma.
Is it right to think that range is for kappa and sigma is for tau?
What scale is the variance (sigma) prior using?

# creating A matrix with spatial nodes and temporal grouping
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
                          loc=as.matrix(wwd.dat[,18:19]),
                          n.spde=spde$n.spde, # number of nodes
                          group=wwd.dat$year, #  grouping variable
                          n.group=n_year) # number of time points

# setting the index for the nodes
field.indices <- inla.spde.make.index("nodes", n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group=n_year)

#creating the inla.stack
stack <- inla.stack(data=list(size= wwd.dat$size),
  A= list(A.est,1),
  effects=
    list(field.indices, ## spacetime index set
         data.frame(
           Intercept=1, ## explicit intercept
           wwd.dat[,9:11])), ## covariates
  tag="est")

Model and output:

I have the space only effect commented out here but I will also present results with the spatial spde only.
#INLA formula
formula <- size ~ -1 + Intercept +  urban + veg_height + moisture + I(urban^2) + I(veg_height^2) +I(moisture^2) +
  # f(nodes,model=spde)
  f(nodes, model=spde, group=nodes.group, control.group=list(model="ar1"))

#model
STmodel <- inla(formula, family= 'poisson',data=inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
  #verbose = TRUE,
  control.predictor=list( A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE),
  control.compute=list( dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, config=TRUE),
    control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", npoints = 21),
    control.results=list( ## save memory not returning all the marginals
    return.marginals.predictor=FALSE,
    return.marginals.random=FALSE))

Space-time model output:

> round(STmodel$summary.hyperpar,2)
                              mean   sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode
Range for nodes    3.76    0.48       2.92     3.72            4.82       3.64
Stdev for nodes    1.69     0.16       1.40     1.68            2.03       1.66
GroupRho for nodes 0.06 0.24      -0.41     0.06           0.53     0.06

 0.0000  0.5105  1.0000  0.7268  1.0000  1.0000

The PIT value histogram is slightly bowled shaped, mostly deformed by a large spike at 0.

Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 1486.75
Effective number of parameters .................: 215.27

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Spatial only model output:

Formula used - #INLA formula
formula <- size ~ -1 + Intercept +
  urban + veg_height + moisture + I(urban^2) + I(veg_height^2) +I(moisture^2) + f(nodes,model=spde)

Note the spatiotemporal term is commented out.

> round(STmodel$summary.hyperpar,2)
                            mean   sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode
Range for nodes 4.33    0.70       3.15       4.26       5.89           4.11
Stdev for nodes  1.71     0.24       1.29       1.69       2.23          1.64

> summary(STmodel$cpo$failure)

The PIT values are not mostly uniform but have a large spike at 1.

Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 1909.56
Effective number of parameters .................: 252.72

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Questions:
What scale is the temporal AR1  Rho parameter in?

Where can I specify the prior for the AR1 term? I can see there is a default horseshoe prior on the AR1 term from the plots of the model output.

Any insight from the above description and code as to why adding the AR1 term results in a massive number of CPO failures? The WAIC score indicates that the AR1 term is quite important.

>

> 2. Partitioning variance between groups in the spatial field.
>
> My motivation is a dataset of animal migration collected over several years. I would like to explore how environmental covariates influence their distribution over this time.
>
> Currently, I have indexed the time mesh to capture the seasonal migration across all years, so I have four time points (one for each season). The spatial field is then fitted as an AR1 process to allow spring (t = 1) to follow winter (t = 4).
>
> However, I have multiple years of point data and a space-time matched covariate that I would like to include in this model. To do this I need to pass data from each of the 5 years to the matched season in the time mesh, so that each time point has 5 replicates. I don’t have data for all seasons and all years and so I don’t want to fit this as a continuous time model – i.e. from spring in year 1 through to winter in year 5.

Hi guys!

I am new to R-INLA and it really looks like a cool and versatile framework.
I wonder if I could use INLA to fit high dimensional Gaussian Process (with 8-20 covariates),
i.e.: f(x) ~ GP(m(x), k(x,x',theta)), which is basically a multi-variate normal
distribution with k(x,x',theta) is a squared exponential covariance function,
basically a function of euclidean distance between two data records (in the high-dimensional
covariate space).

I was searching through the available models - names(inla.models()$latent) - but I only found
SPDE models, i.e. spatial, or spatio-temporal, which thus use only two dimensions (maybe three
including time). I need general N-dimensional one.

So I was researching, how could I maybe implement this into R-INLA myself, hopefully in such a way that
I don't need to understand the internals of the Laplace Approximation, just by defining likelihood and kernel functions.
I found "rgeneric" latent model which allows user to define his own model; but this requires to define function Q
which returns the precision matrix, which effectively means that I would have to directly invert the covariance
matrix. That's too heavy computation burden, which isn't necessary (see GRaF R package or
Rasmussen & Williams 2006: Gaussian processes for machine learning).

So, my question is, how to run these models in R-INLA in most straightforward and simple way?

Thanks a lot!

Tomas

messages.body_plain:
There are several issues.
The gain due to sparsity diminished with both dimension and operator order. The exp(-x^2) covariance, aka squared exponential, corresponds to the limiting case of infinite operator order in the Matérn family, so all benefits are lost. However, in practice, squared.exp. fields are virtually indistinguishable from spades with operator 4 and above. And since the squared.exp. covariance is usually a completely arbitrary choice anyway, you could simply change to such a finite order Matérn model instead.

Inla is geared towards such low order Markov property models, which are very efficient when computations are based on the resulting sparse precision matrices, which keep being sparse when conditioning on data, if the nodes of the model have local direct effect (as they do in the spde/GMRF construction we use). This includes the Cholesky factor. The actual inverse (I.e. the covariance matrix) is not needed, so no full inverse is computed. Any model you can come up with that gives you a sparse precision can take advantage of that.

That leaves the dimension issue, for which there is no universal solution. Regularly gridded data could use a kronecker construction, but there is no built in way to take advantage of that for the posterior precision, which will not have a kronecker structure.

If you really do want very smooth field of the type generated by squared exponential covariances, your best bet is probably to define an rgeneric model based on a finite spectral decomposition. That would give a diagonal prior precision matrix, so no need to invert a covariance matrix in the model definition. The posterior would still have a dense precision, but the dimension of the model could be much smaller than the number of data points.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

inlabru is indeed much more convenient for point processes (and all the Voronoi stuff in the book is really not necessary even in raw R-INLA; it's just a particular way of constructing the approximate likelihood that's needlessly complicated and there's a simpler approach that's also more accurate, sorry about that...)

In James's case he wanted the option of using the spde barrier models that are implemented with rgeneric, which is not currently supported by inlabru (although I expect to add support for it very soon).  I had some further off-list email with James, but I don't recall the details.
As for the time aspect of the model, how to do it best would depend on how many different distinct timepoints should be modelled, and their relative spacing. If there are four seasons, and only a seasonal effect is needed, then having data only for some seasons in different years isn't really an issue.  One just needs to formulate the observation effort for the point process model accordingly; this is similar to how line transect data with overlapping transects (but with long separation in time) just means that the search effort was twice as big in the overlapping part. In inlabru, this is taken care of the "samplers" information, where the user provides as set of lines or polygons (with time information included); the point process likelihood involves the sum of intensity integrals over those search effort polygons. (And _not_ the integral over the union of the polygons; this is the crucial step to get it right.)

Finn

Hi Kevin,

I would suggest working through the inlabru practical exercises, they are where I also started. There is also a great resource in the spde book, that you can access here: https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/

In my case, I am applying INLA to a marine system and would like to constrain my estimation to a complicated coastline boundary. So I have been using Haakon Bakka's barrier model which, as Finn mentions, is not *currently* implemented in inlabru. For more info on the barrier model have a look at the following: https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic107.html

All the best,

James

messages.subject: Re: Space-time indexing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I've had some off-list discussion with Joe Watson and Finn Lindgren. I thought I would share the ideas here for those of you that may run into similar issues in the future.

In my example I've observed a seasonal process over several years, but I don't observe the process in every year. I want to pass the information from each year and season to the model separately rather than aggregating across years as I have a space-time covariate that I want to include.

When generating the data frame to pass to INLA I was aggregating over area and time like this:
agg.dat <- as.data.frame(table(area, time))
Instead, aggregate over area, season and year like so:
agg.dat <- as.data.frame(table(area, season, year))

This then allows the correct space-time covariate information to be passed to the model, and you can proceed as before.

The second issue I had was to pass information from each population separately. The reason for doing this was to allow me to generate separate spatial estimates for each population, as the populations differ in size but have similar observation effort. My ultimate aim is to generate a spatial prediction for the entire population weighted by population size.

Following the example above I can pass the information from each population separately like this:
agg.dat <- as.data.frame(table(area, season, population, year))

These can then get passed to the stack as replicates:

# Create projector matrix
A.st <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = smesh,
                         loc = smesh$loc[agg.dat$area, ],
                         group = agg.dat$season,
                         n.group = k,
                         mesh.group = tmesh,
                         repl = agg.dat$population,
                         n.repl = 3)

# Create space-time index
idx <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 's',

                            n.spde = barrier.model$f$n,
                            n.group = k,
                            n.repl = 3)

stk <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = agg.dat$Freq, exposure = e0),
  A = list(A.st, 1),
  effects = list(idx, list(b0 = rep(1, nrow(agg.dat)))))

However, the resulting model object does not allow me to visualise the spatial field for each population separately. For example, in the way that I can visualise the spatial field for each season separately. Is this possible?

I will likely need to scale the exposure to account for differences in observation effort between years and seasons. My data are from animal telemetry and so there are different numbers of tags deployed in different years, and some tags transmit for longer than others. Instead of visualising the separate spatial fields, could I adjust the exposure for the population size at the same time as adjusting for observational effort?

Best,

James

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have only been actively modelling with INLA since January this year. I am currently running a number of longitudinal models with a Poisson distribution (where time is nested within id) and an error came up when I tried to run the model. I was adjusting the default prior and am testing with (1) informative gamma priors and (2) penalised complexity priors. The following error comes up:

Error in inla.set.hyper(family[i.family], "likelihood", cont.family[[i.family]]$hyper,  :
 Model poisson [ likelihood ], has none hyperparameters, but 'hyper' is  list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma", param = c(0.5, 33.4744778954128)))

# Informative gamma priors
apar <- 0.5
bpar <- apar*var(df12$y, na.rm = T)
lgprior <- list(prec = list(prior="loggamma", param = c(apar,bpar)))

# Model formula
formula_unadj <- y ~ 1 + tot_nat_spa_250 + gender + age + f(id, model = "iid", hyper = lgprior) + f(id_time, model = "iid", hyper = lgprior)

# The model
MI <- inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = df,
                              control.family=list(hyper = lgprior),
                              control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
                              control.compute = list(config=TRUE, dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE), verbose=TRUE)

The error came up when I changed control.family. In my models with default prior, it was control.family=list(variant=0). Once I changed it to control.family=list(hyper=lgprior), the model gives the error above.

My questions:

Might anyone know what is causing the error? The same models with a Gaussian distribution do not produce this error, indicating it has something to do with the family 'Poisson'.
When deleting control family from the model code, the model with family 'Poisson' does run. Is this okay to do? I.e. simply leave out control.family or can this cause other problems? I tried this as it has been done in a book called 'Bayesian regression modelling with INLA' (p 132).
I look forward to hearing from you.

Best wishes,

Mikaël Maes
